date.note: This is a literary and thematic grouping in the Sinai narrative, not an independent datable event. No absolute year is inferred.

claims.claim: Leviticus 8 depicts washing, priestly clothing, anointing, sacrifice, and seven days of ordination.
Leviticus 9 narrates inaugural offerings and the appearance of divine fire consuming the altar offering.
claims.evidence: Lev 9:1–24; narrated event, not independently dated.

claims.claim: Leviticus 10 identifies Nadab and Abihu’s act as presenting fire not commanded by YHWH.
claims.evidence: Lev 10:1–2; the biblical text does not state that they were drunk.

claims.claim: Competing reconstructions of Nadab and Abihu’s precise offense include intoxication, improper incense or fire, timing, and unauthorized approach, but Leviticus 10:1–2 does not specify any such explanation.
claims.evidence: Lev 10:1–11 (KJV); Pittman 2024 Themelios 49(3) 579–588, publisher full article sections 1–4 contrasts Bibb’s gaps reading and Pittman’s proposed unauthorized priestly activity; exact cause and intoxication NOT established. The intoxication hypothesis is surveyed in Pittman n. 1 (Wolak 2013) and the Lev 10:8–11 sequence — sequence only, not a stated cause.

claims.claim: Priests are charged to distinguish holy and common, unclean and clean, and teach Israel.
The contrasting divine fire of Leviticus 9:24 and 10:2 forms a literary juxtaposition about regulated access.
The wilderness narrative of Aaronide priestly installation does not independently establish when Leviticus 8–10 reached its final written form.
claims.evidence: Leviticus 8–10 narrates an installation in the wilderness setting; Exodus 28–29 provides corresponding instructions. Neither biblical passage provides external authentication for the final historical date of its own literary composition; no particular modern dating scheme is asserted. Gane 2022 §3.1 leaves the dating of priestly texts open; narrative setting is not composition evidence.

connections.note: Commands for vestments and consecration correspond to their enactment in Leviticus 8.
The glory fills the completed tabernacle before the priestly inauguration.
The offerings used at inauguration were described earlier.
A later narrative concerns disputed priestly authority.
Priestly and Levitical duties are differentiated.
Ezekiel’s priestly vision echoes holiness and teaching responsibilities.
Christian epistle contrasts Aaronic priesthood with its portrayal of Jesus’s priesthood.
